title: Power Display: Inconsistent triple monitor detection after Maximum Compatibility update

judgment.rationale: The reporter has now confirmed the third monitor is still missing on a latest build and suspects identical monitor names; a second user separately reports USB-C hub displays missing. The exact current version and per-display connection/discovery state are needed to distinguish inventory loss from unsupported control capabilities.
evidence: The original report describes an intermittent missing third display in a triple-monitor setup and unavailable brightness/contrast/volume controls; the original version was PowerToys v0.100.2.

A maintainer said fixes/compatibility improvements would arrive in a later version; the reporter replied that the third monitor is still missing on the latest version and suspects the missing monitor shares a name with another.
A second user reports that PowerToys 0.101 does not detect displays attached through a USB-C hub.
Current Power Display source uses DevicePath-based monitor identity and classifies DisplayConfig inventory into WMI and DDC/CI routes; friendly name is logged separately.
judgment.recommended_action: Request the exact current version and a per-display topology/visibility comparison; use those details to decide whether the failure is inventory discovery or capability routing.

fix_assessment.rationale: A discovery or WMI/DDC route mismatch is plausible, but the current thread combines direct and USB-C-connected monitor reports and lacks the exact topology needed to choose a safe fix.

proposed_fixes.title: Preserve every attached display through Power Display discovery and routing
proposed_fixes.root_cause: A display may be lost between the Windows DisplayConfig inventory and Power Display's WMI/DDC controller classification, particularly on a dock/USB-C path; duplicate friendly names alone are less likely because current monitor identity is based on a DevicePath.
plan: Compare DisplayConfigInventory.GetAllMonitorDisplayInfo output with MonitorManager.DiscoverFromAllControllersAsync classification for the reporter's exact topology.
Trace each display by DevicePath through MonitorIdentity.FromDevicePath and the WMI/DDC route; do not use friendly name or model ID as a unique monitor key.

If a path is dropped or capability-mapped incorrectly, preserve each distinct physical path and report unsupported controls per monitor; add tests for identical model/friendly names and docked displays.
verification: With the reporter's three-monitor topology, verify that every display Windows enumerates appears in Power Display, and that only genuinely unsupported brightness/contrast/volume controls are disabled.

confidence.rationale: The current source separates monitor identity from friendly name, but the report does not identify whether Windows, DisplayConfig, or a Power Display controller omits the third monitor.

issue_context.summary: The original triple-monitor report now has a current confirmation that one display is still missing; another commenter reports a similar detection problem through a USB-C hub, but the exact affected topology and build are not yet known.
known_information: The original report describes a triple-monitor setup where the third display is intermittently absent and some controls are greyed out.
The original report lists PowerToys v0.100.2 and Windows build 26200.8973.
A maintainer promised compatibility fixes in a later version; the reporter subsequently says the latest version still misses the third monitor and suggests two monitors may share a name.
Another commenter separately reports that PowerToys 0.101 misses displays attached to a USB-C hub.
The current code's MonitorIdentity derives Monitor.Id from Windows DevicePath, while MonitorManager classifies DisplayConfig inventory into WMI and DDC/CI routes.
inferences: A duplicate friendly name is not by itself proof of a collision because the inspected Power Display identity is DevicePath-based.
The missing display may be absent from the Windows inventory or lost during Power Display's controller/capability routing; current evidence does not select between them.
issue_context.analysis: The previous artifact's author-wait state is no longer valid: the reporter responded that the issue persists after the promised update. A targeted monitor-topology request can determine whether Windows itself enumerates the display and whether the failure correlates with repeated models, a dock path, or controller capability.
initial_investigation: Read the full issue body and all four comments, including the maintainer's later-version statement, the author's latest-build confirmation, and the separate USB-C hub report.

Inspected current src/modules/powerdisplay/PowerDisplay.Lib/Services/MonitorManager.cs and Models/MonitorIdentity.cs: discovery starts from DisplayConfig inventory, routes by DevicePath, and supports distinct physical devices that share an EDID/model ID.
No covering upstream PR, current fix, or configured MuyuanMS/PowerToys mirror was found; the earlier maintainer comment did not link a concrete fix.

information_gaps.information: For the original reporter's current setup, the model/name and direct-versus-dock/USB-C connection of each display, whether Windows Display Settings lists all three, and which display Power Display omits.
information_gaps.why_needed: This distinguishes a Windows/DisplayConfig enumeration failure from Power Display's WMI/DDC capability routing and tests whether the suspected same-name displays are actually distinct device paths.
information_gaps.how_to_collect: List each display's model and connection path and compare the count/names in Windows Settings > System > Display with PowerToys > Power Display; omit serial numbers.

information_gaps.information: The exact PowerToys About version on which the reporter most recently confirmed the missing display.
information_gaps.why_needed: The original report is from 0.100.2 and the latest reply does not name the build, so it is not possible to verify which compatibility changes were tested.
information_gaps.how_to_collect: Read the version from PowerToys About and include it with the same topology comparison.

comment.body:
Thanks for confirming that the third display is still missing on a later build and for noting that it may share a name with another monitor. Another user separately reports a USB-C-hub case, so the connection path matters.

**Needed**
1. Please provide the exact PowerToys About version.
2. List each monitor model and whether it is connected directly or through a dock/USB-C hub; omit serial numbers.
3. Confirm whether Windows Settings > System > Display shows all three, and identify which one Power Display omits.

This will distinguish a Windows display-enumeration gap from Power Display's controller/capability routing and test whether the same-name suspicion is relevant.

status.label: Confirm Power Display monitor topology
status.detail: The report persists after a later version, but the missing-display boundary and connection path are not established.

next_action.label: Confirm Power Display monitor topology
next_action.reason: Use the exact version and Windows-versus-Power-Display monitor lists to select the failing discovery stage.
